article_title: Schools Can't Do It Alone: Developing Sustainable Systems of Care for School-Based Behavioral Health in California
citation: Caparas, R., Eisenberg, L., Krausen, K., & Lias, C. (2024). Schools can't do it alone: Developing sustainable systems of care for school-based behavioral health in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Student Behavioral Health Incentive Program (SBHIP)
description: The SBHIP is a California short-term initiative that provided more than $389 million over a 3-year period (January 1, 2022, through December 31, 2024) for targeted interventions aimed at increasing access to school-affiliated behavioral health services for TK–12 students in public schools. Funds were distributed to participating Medi-Cal managed care plans, which were required to partner with county offices of education and LEAs. Participating counties conducted student behavioral health needs assessments and developed project plans for using the funds.
requirements: MCPs must partner with COEs and LEAs to facilitate LEAs' program participation
LEAs must identify strategies to sustain new programs after the initiative concludes
constraints: The initiative is short term, ending in December 2024, and does not provide funding to all LEAs and schools across California
target_learners: TK–12 students in California public schools
target_learning_goals: Increased access to school-affiliated behavioral health services
examples: Nearly 60 LEAs across 28 counties submitted SBHIP needs assessments and project plans analyzed in this brief

article_title: What a Systematic Review of 32 Evaluations Says about the Impact of School-Based Law Enforcement
citation: Fisher, B., & Petrosino, A. (2022). What a systematic review of 32 evaluations says about the impact of school-based law enforcement. WestEd. https://jprc.wested.org
title: Crime-deterrence logic and its hypothesized unintended consequences as competing accounts of SBLE effects
description: The brief frames SBLE evaluation around two competing accounts. The deterrence logic "posits that crime is less likely to occur if a potential offender perceives a high risk that they will be caught," predicting reduced misbehavior, improved safety perceptions, and secondary benefits like attendance and test scores. The unintended-consequences account predicts overuse of the formal justice system for school-resolvable behavior, increased fear, and greater detection of offenses, harming perceptions and learning. The review's findings support the second account for discipline outcomes.
requirements: Quantitative evaluations comparing units with SBLE to units without SBLE, at student or school level, to test the competing predictions
constraints: The brief notes many included studies used designs that do not permit strong causal inferences and no randomized control trial findings were available yet
target_learners: K-12 students in schools with school-based law enforcement
target_learning_goals: learning outcomes such as achievement and attendance
examples: The review examined over 16,000 reports and included 32 studies with 1,002 effect sizes, estimating student-level and school-level effects separately
key_sources: Fisher, B., & Petrosino, A. (2022). What a systematic review of 32 evaluations says about the impact of school-based law enforcement. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621156

article_title: What a Systematic Review of 32 Evaluations Says about the Impact of School-Based Law Enforcement
citation: Fisher, B., & Petrosino, A. (2022). What a systematic review of 32 evaluations says about the impact of school-based law enforcement. WestEd. https://jprc.wested.org
title: Do not expect SBLE to improve school safety or learning; expect increased student punishment instead
description: Based on its synthesis, the brief advises that SBLE's documented effect is punitive rather than protective: "SBLE contributes to increased punishment of students without providing improvements in school safety." Decision-makers weighing SBLE adoption or retention should therefore not expect crime prevention or learning gains from officer presence alone, and should weigh the discipline increases against the absence of safety or learning benefits.
requirements: Districts considering SBLE should consult evaluation evidence comparing units with and without SBLE rather than relying on deterrence expectations alone
constraints: The brief cautions that many included studies used designs that do not permit strong causal inferences, and no randomized control trial findings were available yet
target_learners: K-12 students in schools with or considering school-based law enforcement
target_learning_goals: learning outcomes such as achievement and attendance
examples: The review's synthesis of 32 evaluations found higher exclusionary discipline with SBLE and no significant relationships with learning outcomes or most crime outcomes

article_title: SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging
citation: Zhiwei Yang, Jiahua Yang, Huiru Lin, Xing Chen, and Quanlong Guan. (2026). SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36982
title: S Bio and S Phy: two new knowledge concept tagging datasets for cross-discipline validation
description: The authors constructed two new benchmark datasets to address the lack of validation data outside mathematics: "we construct two new datasets, i.e., S Bio and S Phy, which will be made available to fill the gap in cross-validation of knowledge concept tagging methods across different disciplines". S Bio contains 9,941 exercises with 72 concept categories for grades 10-12, and S Phy contains 18,440 exercises with 135 categories for grades 10-12; both include questions, solutions, difficulty scores, and knowledge concepts, split 8:1:1 into training, validation and test sets with balanced concept distributions. Unsupervised corpora U Bio (15,669) and U Phy (32,138) support continued pre-training.
requirements: Labeled exercises with questions, solutions, difficulty scores and knowledge concept annotations, split stratified by concept category
constraints: Both datasets cover grades 10-12 biology and physics in a Chinese educational context
target_learners: senior secondary (grades 10-12) biology and physics students whose exercises are tagged
target_learning_goals: fine-grained knowledge concept tagging of exercises to support knowledge tracing, cognitive diagnosis and recommendation
examples: The datasets were used to evaluate SRJudge and all baselines alongside the existing S Math dataset

article_title: Simulation-Based Education to Support Nurses' Critical Thinking in Delirium Recognition: A Scoping Review.
citation: EL Hussein Mohamed Toufic, Sheehan Dawson S., Hirst Sandra. (2026). Simulation‐Based Education to Support Nurses' Critical Thinking in Delirium Recognition: A Scoping Review. Journal of Advanced Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.70640
title: Four interrelated domains of critical thinking developed through simulation for delirium recognition
description: The review organizes its synthesis around four interrelated domains through which simulation-based education develops critical thinking: cue recognition, clinical reasoning, metacognitive reflection, and communication and advocacy. The authors state that "simulation‐based education supports the development of critical thinking through four interrelated domains", each contributing uniquely to detecting, interpreting and acting on subtle, fluctuating delirium cues. The framework is anchored in Facione's critical-thinking definition, Tanner's Clinical Judgement Model stages of noticing, interpreting, responding and reflecting, and Kolb's experiential learning theory, positioning clinical reasoning as "not a linear sequence but an adaptive, context‐dependent skill".
requirements: Structured pre-briefings and debriefings, deliberate cue exposure and opportunities for reflection on diagnostic reasoning, emotional regulation and communication, per the review's implications section.
constraints: No included study directly measured critical thinking as an explicit outcome; the domains are extrapolated from consistent improvements in reasoning, reflection and decision accuracy.
target_learners: Practicing registered nurses in adult clinical settings
examples: The review maps SP/OSCE simulations to cue recognition and screening accuracy, VR and theatre-based modalities to empathy and reflection, and multimodal programmes to documentation and communication behaviour change.

article_title: The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students' knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review.
citation: Alharbi, A., Nurfianti, A., Mullen, R. F., McClure, J. D., & Miller, W. H. (2024). The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students’ knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06080-z
title: Three-theme framework for synthesising SBL effects: acquisition, retention, and wider clinical performance
description: The review organises its narrative synthesis into three themes interpreting SBL's impact on nursing students. The first theme, "Impact of SBL on knowledge and skills acquisition", probes immediate effects on learner capabilities; the second, "Impact of SBL on retention of knowledge and skills", examines durability over time; the third, "Impact of SBL on wider clinical performance", concerns broader practice outcomes including self-confidence, satisfaction, clinical reasoning, self-efficacy and problem-solving. The framework structures how the review's 33 studies are compared across designs, interventions and outcome measures.
requirements: Studies must report knowledge, skills acquisition and/or retention outcomes in nursing student populations to be synthesised under the framework
constraints: The retention theme lacks universality due to limited long-term analyses and mixed results, as the review states
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate nursing students
target_learning_goals: clinical performance behaviours such as teamwork and self-efficacy
examples: The review categorises findings from 33 studies into the three themes, e.g., CPR skill gains under Theme 1, four-month BLS retention under Theme 2, and teamwork improvements under Theme 3

article_title: The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students' knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review.
citation: Alharbi, A., Nurfianti, A., Mullen, R. F., McClure, J. D., & Miller, W. H. (2024). The effectiveness of simulation-based learning (SBL) on students’ knowledge and skills in nursing programs: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education, 24. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06080-z
title: Use simulation-based learning as a core teaching strategy in nursing education while continuing to evaluate and refine it
description: The review concludes that simulation-based learning is a potent teaching strategy within nursing education, supporting its use for building knowledge and clinical skills in safe, realistic environments. It pairs this endorsement with the requirement for "the ongoing evaluation and refinement of this approach", since acquisition evidence is stronger than retention evidence. Educators adopting SBL should therefore treat it as an evidence-supported but still-evolving method whose design, implementation and evaluation need continued study.
requirements: Ongoing evaluation and refinement of SBL interventions, as the review's conclusion states
constraints: Limited studies evaluated retention beyond five months, constraining generalisable claims regarding durability
Heterogeneity of study designs, risk of bias, and lack of long-term follow-up limit the evidence base
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate nursing students
examples: The review's 33 included studies implemented SBL via high-, medium- and low-fidelity manikins, virtual simulation, serious games and virtual reality across CPR, critical care and decision-making topics

article_title: Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review.
citation: Yun Jungmi, Lee Yun Ji, Kang Kyoungrim, Park Jongmin. (2023). Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04495-8
title: SBAR as a structured communication framework for clinical handover
description: SBAR (situation, background, assessment, recommendation) is a structured communication tool comprising "the communication of the patient's current situation, the background and causes of the situation, the assessment of the current condition, and the reporter's recommendations for further treatment." The review describes it as reliable, validated, easily implemented in hospital practice, and enabling clear communication in a short time. It is the intervention core of the simulation programs reviewed, embedded in scenarios, role-play, and reports.
requirements: Training programs must teach all four SBAR components so users perform SBAR as intended (fidelity)
constraints: The review notes programs in the included literature did not incorporate surveillance or monitoring of fidelity to SBAR
target_learners: nursing students
examples: Included programs embedded SBAR in orientation, lectures, role-play, scenario simulation, and debriefing, with durations between one and six hours
key_sources: Yun Jungmi, Lee Yun Ji, Kang Kyoungrim, Park Jongmin. (2023). Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04495-8

article_title: Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review.
citation: Yun Jungmi, Lee Yun Ji, Kang Kyoungrim, Park Jongmin. (2023). Effectiveness of SBAR-based simulation programs for nursing students: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04495-8
title: SBAR simulation programs combine pre-briefing, role-play simulation, and debriefing/discussion over one to six hours
description: The reviewed interventions shared a recurring structure: "The interventions included in the analysis consisted of orientation, pre-briefing, role-play simulation, debriefing, or discussion." Program duration varied between one and six hours; in 8 studies pre-briefing lasted more than 60 minutes, and most Korean programs included at least 60 minutes of orientation, lecture, or education before scenario performance with role-play. Control conditions ranged from e-learning and self-learning to regular clinical practice and conventional lectures.
requirements: Sufficient pre-briefing time (more than 60 minutes in 8 of the included studies) before scenario performance
constraints: Programs differed in intervention period, components, and measurement methods, preventing integrated comparison of effects
target_learners: nursing students in clinical training
examples: One study applied a four-phase clinical practicum with SBAR training (concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualization, active experimentation); another used a three-session program of 20-minute education, 15–20-minute role-play, and 10-minute group discussion

article_title: Performance effects of simulation training for medical students - a systematic review.
citation: McInerney Niall, Nally D., Khan M.F., Heneghan H., Cahill R.A. (2022). Performance effects of simulation training for medical students – a systematic review. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2022-39/zma001572.shtml
title: Simulation-based medical education (SBME) as an adjunct to traditional undergraduate medical curricula
description: SBME uses a "device that presents a simulated patient (or part of a patient) that interacts appropriately with the actions taken by the simulation participant", allowing students to learn in a safe, controlled and standardised environment. Methods reviewed include artificial patient models such as SimMan (median 17.5 minutes per session) and standardized patients (median 82.5 minutes per session). The review validates SBME as an adjunct to the traditional didactic lecture-based curriculum for undergraduate medical students.
requirements: Requires investment in terms of teaching personnel, equipment and space, which the review states makes objective proof of usefulness important to justify expenditure
constraints: Evidence covers knowledge-based performance at least in the short term; longer-term impacts and cost-effectiveness remain unassessed per the review's conclusion
target_learners: undergraduate medical students, first to final year, in general medicine and surgery
examples: The review synthesised nineteen studies using mannequin simulators, standardized patients and hybrid models, assessed by written examinations, checklists and OSCEs.

article_title: The Effect of Schema-vs-Translation-Based Instruction on Persian Medical Students' Learning of General English
citation: Ebrahim Khodadady, Majid Elahi. (2012). The Effect of Schema-Vs-Translation-Based Instruction on Persian Medical Students' Learning of General English. English Language Teaching, 5(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n1p146
title: 120-item schema-based cloze multiple choice item test (SBCMCIT) developed on the course textbook
description: A 120-item schema-based cloze multiple choice item test developed on the first four units of English for the Students of Medicine I. Its competitives were chosen from 360 of the 1892 semantic schemata parsed from the texts, giving it construct and content validity. Piloted on 16 general English students, it reached an Alpha reliability of .83 as pretest and .96 as posttest, and served as both pretest and posttest in the study.
requirements: Schemata comprising the taught texts are parsed and assigned to semantic, syntactic and parasyntactic domains so alternatives share semantic features with the keyed response.
constraints: Items were piloted for p-values between .25 and .75 and point-biserial correlations of .20 or higher following Baker (1989).
target_learners: undergraduate medical students of general English
target_learning_goals: vocabulary and structure knowledge of taught texts
examples: The appendix gives the full test, built on passages about malaria, influenza and measles, with schema-based competitives for each deleted word.

article_title: Effects of a Research-Based Intervention to Improve Seventh-Grade Students' Proportional Problem Solving: A Cluster Randomized Trial
citation: Jitendra, A. K., Harwell, M. R., Dupuis, D. N., Karl, S. R., Lein, A. E., Simonson, G., & Slater, S. C. (2015). Effects of a research-based intervention to improve seventh-grade students’ proportional problem solving: A cluster randomized trial. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000039
title: Schema-based instruction theoretical framework: an elaboration of schema theory integrating four instructional components
description: SBI's theoretical framework is "an elaboration of schema theory" guided by cognitive models of mathematical problem solving (Mayer, 1999). The intervention integrates four major components: a focus on the mathematical structure of problems, use of visual representations (schematic diagrams), explicit problem solving and metacognitive strategy instruction, and an emphasis on procedural flexibility. These components correspond with What Works Clearinghouse recommendations and address CCSS mathematical practices. Instruction uses the four-step DISC strategy (Discover the problem type, Identify information, Solve, Check) with teacher modeling, scaffolded dialogues, and deep-level questions.
requirements: Teachers require professional development (16 hours in this study) to learn to sort problems by type, use schematic diagrams, generate estimates, and select among multiple solution strategies
constraints: The framework was evaluated for seventh-grade proportional problem solving involving ratios/rates and percents; effects did not extend to a standardized general mathematics measure in this study
target_learners: seventh-grade middle school students
target_learning_goals: proportional reasoning with ratios, rates, and percents
problem solving and metacognitive strategy use
procedural flexibility in selecting solution methods
examples: Teachers replaced lessons on ratio/proportion and percent with two SBI replacement units of ten 50-min lessons each, using schematic diagrams and the DISC four-step strategy

article_title: Investigating a Tier 1 Intervention Focused on Proportional Reasoning: A Follow-Up Study
citation: Jitendra, A. K., Harwell, M. R., Karl, S. R., Im, S-H., & Slater, S. C. (2017). Investigating a Tier 1 intervention focused on proportional reasoning: A follow-up study. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 83(4), 340-358. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402917691017
title: Schema-based instruction (SBI) for proportional reasoning
description: SBI is a Tier 1 mathematics intervention built around four instructional practices: "(a) problem structure identification, (b) problem representation using schematic diagrams, (c) procedural flexibility, and (d) problem solving and metacognitive strategy knowledge application." Students learn a seven-step problem solving sequence from recognizing the problem type to checking the reasonableness of the solution, with metacognitive monitoring and reflection on when, how, and why to use multiple strategies. The program comprises 21 lessons across Ratio/Proportion and Percent units, uses real-world scenarios, whole-class instruction and Think/Plan-Share partner work, and was implemented here with 2 days (16 hr) of teacher professional development.
requirements: Teachers received 2 days (16 hr) of professional development covering SBI principles, materials, and implementation practices including video demonstrations
constraints: In this study the intervention was implemented 45 minutes daily for 6 weeks in late October, earlier in the school year than the original study
target_learners: seventh-grade students with and without mathematics difficulties
examples: Treatment teachers taught two units (Ratio and Proportion; Percent) using SBI curriculum materials including a detailed teacher guide, visual diagrams, problem solving checklists, and student workbook and homework books

citation: Loukaitou-Sideris, A. (2015). Targeting the Body and the Mind: Evaluation of a P.E. Curriculum Intervention for Adolescents. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 3(4). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v3i4.873
title: Station-rotation format with small-group equipment-based activities
description: The SBSM curriculum organizes each of thirty lessons into Warm-up, Workout, and Cool Down sessions, with the Workout at 4-6 stations where student groups rotate through equipment-based physical tasks. Activities are "designed for small spaces" and do not require gyms, fitting inner-city school constraints. Teachers reported the rotating-station format engaged all students simultaneously.
requirements: P.E. equipment including balls, cones, free-weights, jumping ropes, exercise mats, agility ladders, and marking tape
constraints: Class duration limits rotations to 3-6 per session depending on P.E. class length
target_learners: Adolescent students in grades 7-10 in inner-city schools

citation: Jitendra, A. K., Harwell, M. R., Karl, S. R., Dupuis, D. N., Simonson, G., Slater, S. C., & Lein, A. E. (2016). Learning and Instruction, 44, 53-64. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2016.03.001
title: Schema-based instruction (SBI): a multicomponent intervention emphasizing the mathematical structure of problems through schematic diagrams with problem solving and metacognitive strategy instruction
description: Schema-based instruction (SBI) is a multicomponent intervention rooted in schema theory of cognitive psychology and cognitive models of mathematical problem solving. The article describes SBI as "a multicomponent intervention that emphasizes the mathematical structure of problems through the use of schematic diagrams and incorporates problem solving and metacognitive strategy instruction." The SBI program comprises 21 lessons across two units (Ratio/Proportion and Percent) and rests on four instructional practices: modeling problem solving and metacognitive strategies, activating the mathematical structure of problems, visually mapping information using schematic diagrams, and developing procedural flexibility.
requirements: Teachers are guided to use effective instructional practices (e.g., explicit modeling, guided questions to engage students) to help students recognize the problem type, represent the problem using a diagram, solve the problem, and check the solution.
constraints: Lessons were scripted to provide a detailed teaching procedure, but teachers were asked not to read the scripts verbatim.
target_learners: seventh-grade students learning ratios, proportion, and percent
examples: Teachers taught the two SBI units daily for 50 min a day for approximately six weeks during regularly scheduled seventh-grade mathematics classes.

SBL provides a psychologically safe environment where students can "make mistakes without the risk of overexposing the patient" before transitioning to real patients.

title: SBL in oral radiology is underpinned by Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, situated learning, communities of practice, and Kolb's experiential learning
description: The article frames mannequin-based SBL within social and experiential learning theories. Vygotsky's zone of proximal development underpins structured supervision, where "tutors scaffold students' learning by offering step-by-step demonstrations, corrective feedback, and opportunities for repeated practice." Situated learning and communities of practice (Lave and Wenger) frame the simulation lab as a social context where students collaborate, observe peers, and exchange feedback. Kolb's experiential learning explains learning through observing, performing, linking knowledge, and using tutor feedback and self-reflection.
requirements: Instructor scaffolding with demonstrations, corrective feedback, and repeated practice opportunities
A social learning context where students learn from peers in communities of practice
constraints: The framework is presented as a conceptual lens for the study rather than a tested model
target_learners: undergraduate dental students
examples: The simulation oral radiology lab functioned as a community of practice where students actively collaborated, observed peers, exchanged feedback, and collectively refined their radiographic skills

article_title: Effect of scenario-based simulation on students' learning outcomes and satisfaction in perioperative anaphylaxis: a pilot randomised controlled trial.
citation: Yang Xiuli, Jiang Hui, Wang Huan, Wang Lixia, Chen Lijian. (2026). Effect of scenario-based simulation on students’ learning outcomes and satisfaction in perioperative anaphylaxis: a pilot randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open Quality. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjoq-2025-003713
title: Integrate scenario-based simulation into anaesthesia curricula to prepare students for high-stakes, low-frequency emergencies such as perioperative anaphylaxis
description: The article recommends integrating scenario-based simulation into anaesthesia education because simulation "allows medical students to cope with rare, high-risk incidents in safe and controlled environments" and enhances active engagement. In the trial, SBS sessions included briefing, facilitation and debriefing with role assignment (anaesthesiologist, surgeon, nurse anaesthetist, circulating nurse) and structured debriefing by an observing instructor. The authors state this could "enhance preparedness for high-stakes, low-frequency emergencies like perioperative anaphylaxis".
requirements: Requires a simulation lab with a full-body adult patient simulator, orientation to simulator features, and an instructor who observes without intervention and conducts a structured debriefing afterwards.
constraints: The authors note the benefits were shown in a pilot study with a small sample, and further research is required to investigate transfer of competencies to real-world clinical settings across broader specialties and multidisciplinary teams.
target_learners: fourth-year undergraduate anaesthesia students

Debriefing sessions follow each simulation, where learners "reflect on their performance, identify areas for improvement, and receive constructive instructor feedback"

article_title: Pre-clerkship procedural training in venipuncture: a prospective cohort study on skills acquisition and durability.
citation: Kodikara Kaumudee, Seneviratne Thilanka, Premaratna Ranjan. (2023). Pre-clerkship procedural training in venipuncture: a prospective cohort study on skills acquisition and durability. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04722-2
title: Pre-clerkship simulation-based venipuncture training program with hybrid simulators, Peyton's Four-Step Approach, and mastery-learning feedback
description: A two-hour skills-laboratory training session for small groups of 3-4 students per hybrid simulator, combining a part-task trainer for technical venipuncture skills with standardized patients for communication role-play. Instruction followed "Rodney Peyton's 'Four-Step Approach'"; communication practice drew on the ALOBA scheme. Students practiced as many times as desired and "iteratively received direct feedback and targeted practice on the steps that were not achieved until they could independently complete the entire procedure", per mastery learning practices.
requirements: Hybrid simulators pairing a part-task trainer with standardized patients
Instructors providing direct, specific feedback on technical performance and communication
Small groups of 3-4 students per simulator
constraints: Opportunities for redundant training and deliberate practice were virtually nonexistent in the resource-limited local context
Skills taught in the pre-clinical phase were not formally assessed and not revisited in following years
target_learners: Pre-clerkship (second-year) medical students
examples: All 55 second-year students trained on a Laerdal Multi-Venous IV Training Arm with SP role-play, then were assessed with the IPPI by a blinded independent assessor

article_title: Time for a simulation strategy?
citation: Shiner N. (2023). Time for a simulation strategy? Journal of Medical Radiation Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1002/jmrs.685
title: Simulation-based education underpinned by experiential and cognitive load theory
description: The editorial states that "The use of simulation is underpinned by theory". Considering experiential theory, simulation offers an opportunity to reach mastery in a skill, technique, or scenarios, though mastery does not come with one-off simulations. Considering cognitive load theory, educators should ensure a scaffolded approach, offering a reduced-risk environment before clinical practice. VR offers repeated practice opportunities whereas traditional simulation is more time and staff intensive.
requirements: Planning the frequency of simulation in the curriculum, since mastery does not come with one-off simulations
constraints: Traditional simulation is more time and staff intensive, which can limit its use
target_learners: Undergraduate radiography students
target_learning_goals: Skill mastery and preparation for clinical practice
examples: The editorial links the five-stage scaffolded model to cognitive load theory and notes VR's affordance for repeated practice.

article_title: Simulation-Based Mastery Learning Improves the Performance of Donning and Doffing of Personal Protective Equipment by Medical Students.

Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2022.2.54748
title: Simulation-based mastery learning: an instructional model with seven standard components culminating in advancement only after a mastery standard is reached
description: SBML is described as an educational model that "ensures all trainees meet a high, pre-defined standard for the learning." The article lists seven components: "clearly defined learning objectives; a minimum passing standard (MPS) for proficiency; baseline skills testing using a standardized assessment; engagement in an educational activity with deliberate practice of a skill with expert feedback; post-testing to determine whether the MPS for mastery was achieved; continued practice until the mastery standard is reached; and advancement to the next educational activity only once the mastery standard is reached."
requirements: Requires a pre-defined minimum passing standard set by standard-setting (here a Mastery Angoff standard), standardized assessment checklists, and trained faculty facilitators who deliver deliberate practice with expert feedback.
constraints: Two of 153 students did not reach mastery when deliberate-practice time was capped by institutional scheduling constraints.
target_learners: Medical students (pre-clinical and clinical)
target_learning_goals: Procedural skills such as PPE donning and doffing, and other clinical procedures
examples: The study applied SBML to PPE training: baseline testing, deliberate practice with at least one expert demonstration and targeted feedback, and post-testing until the 21/21 MPS was met.

title: Medical schools should adopt SBML for PPE training before clinical experiences because standard video-based training leaves students unproficient
description: The article recommends that "medical schools should strongly consider using SBML when designing PPE training for medical students," since standard training generally "offers little if any skills practice, thus reducing its success in providing procedural competency." SBML pairs deliberate practice with expert feedback and proficiency testing, which the authors note increases procedural skill retention compared to practice alone.
requirements: Simulation supplies, trained faculty facilitator-raters, a standardized checklist with a minimum passing standard, and sufficient session time for deliberate practice.
constraints: Deliberate practice and proficiency testing require significant faculty time; findings come from a single institution and a simulated environment without randomization.
target_learners: Medical students ahead of clinical experiences
target_learning_goals: Procedural proficiency in PPE donning and doffing to prevent occupational exposures
examples: After SBML, 151/153 students met the 21/21 standard whereas almost all failed after CDC video training alone.

article_title: Exploration of simulation-based medical education for undergraduate students.
citation: Wang S, Ren X, Ye J, Wang W, Huang H, Qin C. (2021). Exploration of simulation-based medical education for undergraduate students. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000025982
title: Clinical-scenario simulation practice with web-based preview and teacher-guided debriefing
description: This lesson-level pattern replaces demonstration-first practice with scenario-based simulation: students preview content via web-based learning, then practice clinical operations on molds or a human phantom within clinical scenarios, discussing and deciding the next action while the teacher guides them to find, think about, and solve problems themselves. The article states that "The practice began with clinical scenarios, in which the teacher added the content of practice," and that the "Muke." app was interspersed throughout the whole SBME process. Four printed cases (wound closure, infected dressing change, drainage-tube removal, CPR) each pair training items such as aseptic concept, doctor–patient communication, and teamwork with a preparation and teaching process ending in discussion and feedback.
requirements: A clinical teacher leads each session of about 10 students
Web-based preview material (the Muke app) available between study and practice sessions
Molds or a human phantom for the clinical operations
Debriefing and feedback after practice
constraints: The article notes standard assessment tools for SBME are still missing and a uniform measurement way is full of limitations
target_learners: Undergraduate junior medical students learning surgery
examples: Students received web-based learning using the Muke app between study and practice sessions, then practiced tension suture, suture tying, CPR, dressing change, and drainage-tube removal within four printed clinical cases
key_sources: Wang S, Ren X, Ye J, Wang W, Huang H, Qin C. (2021). Exploration of simulation-based medical education for undergraduate students. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000025982

article_title: Cohort study of hospitalists' procedural skills: baseline competence and durability after simulation-based training.
citation: Hale Caleb, Crocker Jonathan, Vanka Anita, Ricotta Daniel N, McSparron Jakob I, Huang Grace C. (2021). Cohort study of hospitalists' procedural skills: baseline competence and durability after simulation-based training. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8370503/
title: One-on-one 60-minute simulation-based mastery learning intervention for lumbar puncture and abdominal paracentesis using Peyton's four-step model
description: The intervention was one-on-one, 60-minute SBML for each procedure delivered by one of three instructors, "employing Peyton's four-step model of procedure training as an educational framework". Training began with published procedure videos, then instructor demonstration with verbalised checklist steps, then participant practice on the simulator with direct, specific feedback. In accordance with mastery learning practices, participants practiced iteratively with targeted feedback on unachieved steps until they independently completed the entire procedure at the MPS (18/21 for LP, 21/25 for AP).
requirements: Requires trained instructors, procedural simulators usable for both training and assessment, published checklists with predetermined minimum passing scores (18 of 21 for LP, 21 of 25 for AP), and published procedure videos
constraints: The article reports a single episode of this training was insufficient to sustain skills for the majority of hospitalists over about 7 months in the setting of low procedural volumes
target_learners: credentialed hospitalists who supervise trainees performing invasive bedside procedures
target_learning_goals: technical competence in lumbar puncture and abdominal paracentesis to a minimum passing standard
examples: Twenty-two hospitalists completed baseline videotaped simulator assessment, then the 60-minute SBML session, with 100% reaching the MPS immediately after training

article_title: Simulation-based education for selected communication skills: exploring the perception of post-graduate dental students.
citation: Mascarenhas Sharon, Al-Halabi Manal, Otaki Farah, Nasaif Mohamed, Davis Dave. (2021). Simulation-based education for selected communication skills: exploring the perception of post-graduate dental students. Korean J Med Educ 33(1):11-25. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2021.183
title: Design SBE for adult learners' communication skills in alignment with adult learning theory and Kolb's experiential learning cycle, considering learners, their experiences, and environments
description: The article recommends grounding simulation-based education for post-graduate professionals in adult learning theory (self-directed, intrinsically motivated learners with prior mental models) and Kolb's experiential learning cycle, after thorough consideration of the individual learners, their experiences, and learning environments. The intervention ensured "offering the learners a concrete experience, followed by abstract conceptualization where the learners further develop their own mental models". The authors conclude such theory-based SBE "holds potential in enhancing communication skills among post-graduate dental students".
requirements: Learners assumed to be self-directed and capable of self-regulation, with voluntary enrollment
Debriefing designed to maximize reflecting and reconsidering prior knowledge and mental models
Pre-reading materials and policies provided as complementary learning resources
constraints: The case-study design limited generalizability of the results; findings rest on perceptions from a single institution
target_learners: post-graduate dental students
adult learners in health professions education
examples: MBRU's Hamdan Bin Mohammed College of Dental Medicine piloted the SBE opportunity across all enrolled students in five specialties, with scenarios based on previously acquired knowledge and past learning experiences

article_title: Simulation-based training of junior doctors in handling critically ill patients facilitates the transition to clinical practice: an interview study.
citation: Søren Marker, Marlene Mohr, Doris Østergaard. (2019). Simulation-based training of junior doctors in handling critically ill patients facilitates the transition to clinical practice: an interview study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1447-0
title: A 4-day simulation-based course combining short lectures, workshops, scenario-based simulation and structured debriefing prepares first-year doctors for managing critically ill patients
description: The mandatory course runs 4 days across the first two months of clinical practice, combining short lectures, workshops and SBT scenarios of around 20 minutes followed by feedback or three-phase debriefing (description, analysis, application). Teams of five doctors role-play first-year doctor, senior doctor and nurses. The article reports that "The balance between theory and praxis and the time for reflection generates optimal outcome from the course".
requirements: Instructors certified in SBT and in conducting feedback/debriefings
A safe learning environment without risk of embarrassment in front of colleagues
Scenario realism, with complexity limited to allow focus on relevant learning goals
constraints: Scenario difficulty needs to be balanced
A low level of updated theoretical medical knowledge impairs focus on non-technical skills learning
Realism depends on participant attitude; if one refuses to play, realism drops heavily
target_learners: first-year doctors in their foundation year
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills such as communication, teamwork, leadership and situational awareness
use of the ABCDE, SBAR and ACCEPT algorithms
examples: Scenarios include simulated patients with acute medical conditions handled by the first-year doctor, with debriefing using video recording clips
Doctors highlighted the importance of a safe learning environment and appreciated the combination of the different methods

article_title: Satisfaction of medical students with simulation based learning.
citation: Agha Sajida, Alhamrani Asma Y., Khan Muhammad A. (2015). Satisfaction of medical students with simulation based learning. Saudi Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.15537/smj.2015.6.11501
title: Self-developed 40-item SBL satisfaction and challenges questionnaire (5-point Likert, alpha 0.73)
description: A self-developed questionnaire assessing medical students' satisfaction with and challenges of simulation based learning, consisting of "40 items related to satisfaction and challenges they faced during simulation teaching" on a 5-point Likert scale, with open-ended follow-up questions. Items covered knowledge, skill, environment, resources, and faculty, and were validated by expert reviewers with reliability alpha 0.73.
requirements: Expert reviewer validation and reliability calculation, as performed by a senior researcher, a biostatistician, and two simulation faculty
constraints: The article states there was a lack of psychometric testing of the instrument
target_learners: third- and fourth-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: evaluating satisfaction with simulation based learning and identifying implementation challenges
examples: Distributed to 185 students with a 62% response rate (n=115), analyzed with descriptive statistics and independent samples t-tests in SPSS version 20
